title: Organs, guitars and drums

lines: A LOW NOTE THROUGH THE FLOOR.
cards: The first note comes up through the floor before it reaches your ears: a low hum in your shoes, then a stone room filled with sound from a wall of metal pipes.
Across town, a drummer clicks his sticks, one, two, three, four, and a guitar and a bass come in under a screen of lyrics. In a third church, there's no instrument at all.
A single voice sings a line, and the room answers it. Ask in any of those rooms what's going on, and you may hear the same answer: praising God with what they have.

teach.b: Start at the end of the Psalms. Psalm one hundred fifty is a list of instruments, and the King James Bible says: "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs."
Organs, right there. But some readers take the Hebrew word behind it as a simple pipe, nothing like a cathedral organ with pedals. The psalm was gathering every sound it knew.

Another psalm says: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise." Churches with guitars, drums and keyboards often point to lines like that. So do churches with pipe organs, which were once new themselves.
Each generation brings the instruments it has. Then, the churches that use none.

teach.h: SOME CHURCHES SING WITH NO INSTRUMENT.
teach.b: Orthodox churches traditionally sing their services without instruments, and so do some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ.

They read Paul's words to the Ephesians: "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." For them, the human voice is the instrument God made. Each of these churches has reasons, and takes them seriously.
Last, the end of that list psalm.

After trumpet, harp, strings, pipes and two kinds of cymbal, it doesn't end on an instrument: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Every instrument on the list depends on breath, and every person has it.

how: Christians worship with pipe organs, pianos, guitars, drums and bands, or with no instruments at all: Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied.

games.q: instruments of praise — tap the pairs.

s: the word organs appears in the King James Psalms
"praise him with stringed instruments and organs." some readers take the Hebrew word behind it as a kind of pipe.
every church uses instruments in worship
Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches, like the Churches of Christ, sing without them.
Psalm 150 ends on the loudest cymbal
it ends on breath: "let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD."

games.q: you're writing the last line of Psalm 150. you've listed trumpet, harp, timbrel, strings, pipes and cymbals. what comes last?
o: one more cymbal, the loudest yet.
games.why: "let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." the list of instruments ends with every living thing.

practice: Play a recording of an organ, a gospel band or a hymn with guitar, and listen for two minutes, noticing where the sound sits in your body: chest, feet, throat.

If you can't play anything, listen to your own breathing, the instrument the psalm ends on. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without words; if you don't, just listen all the way to the end.

wordCard.voice: Organs. The pipes in old churches, a word the King James Psalms already used, and a reminder that churches praise with the sounds they have.

orig.note: Hebrew: the instrument the King James Bible calls organs in Psalm 150, which some readers take as a kind of pipe.

carryVoice: Your line: every instrument praise. The week ran from colors of the year, incense and candles to the cross, icons, hymnals and organs: faith you can see, smell and hear. That's the week.
